interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: How Do Agents Fail on AutoResearch: End-to-End Diagnostic Evaluation on 100 Real-World Frontier Research Tasks
papers.authors: Yanlin Fei , Nazhou Liu , Xinmiao Yu , Shaolong Chen , Lei Li , Rahul Thapa , Madalina Ciobanu , Qingqing Mao , Ritankar Das
papers.abstract: AI has long assisted scientific research, but the rapid advance of LLMs and agentic scaffolds is reshaping the landscape; a single system can now carry whole-stage research from an initial hypothesis all the way to final published paper, which is a paradigm now referred to as AutoResearch. Existing evaluations reveal little about how these agents operate or where they break down. Tasks are narrowly-scoped, evaluation measures performance but not process, and failure diagnoses lack systematic coverage or artifact-level visibility. To address this gap, we introduce AutoResearchEval, featuring 100 tasks grounded in published frontier science across 7 scientific domains and the full research lifecycle, including ideation, retrieval, execution, analysis, writing, and review. Evaluating 8 harness-model combinations yields 800 autoresearch agent trajectories, with process-level annotation. We organize these insights into AutoResearch Failure Taxonomy or ARFT, a framework of 45 empirically-grounded failure patterns. To enable scalable fine-grained attribution, we leverage a human-calibrated agent-as-a-judge pipeline to inspect complete trajectories and intermediate artifacts. Failure patterns converge on a single overarching limitation, namely that current agents lack a metacognitive loop, which entails the ability to check what they produced against what they found, revise when it does not hold up, and question whether the path they took was sound. The same patterns recur across all 8 harness-model combinations, including the strongest models tested, locating the deficit at the model level rather than in any particular scaffold; whether orchestration-level interventions can close it is an open question this work does not test. We publicly release AutoResearchEval and ARFT to facilitate continued research and development in autonomous scientific discovery.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses AutoResearch, which is central to my interest in automated scientific discovery. The failure taxonomy and evaluation on real research tasks are highly relevant for building research agents for astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper introduces AutoResearchEval, a benchmark of 100 real-world research tasks across 7 domains, evaluating agentic research systems end-to-end. The main idea is to provide process-level annotations and a failure taxonomy, finding that agents lack a metacognitive loop. For astronomy, this is highly relevant because it identifies common failure modes in autonomous research, which could inform the design of astronomy-specific agents. A concrete workflow could be using this benchmark to evaluate an agent that analyzes JWST data and writes papers. The main caveat is that the tasks are not astronomy-specific, so the failure patterns may differ in scientific domains with specialized data.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the failure taxonomy includes domain-specific issues, such as data handling or visualization
Look for any details on the agent-as-a-judge pipeline, which could be used for evaluating astronomical research agents

papers.title: Personalized Auto-Research: Towards a True AI Co-Scientist
papers.authors: Bo Ni , Franck Dernoncourt , Hongjie Chen , Yu Wang , Nesreen K. Ahmed , Zhengzhong Tu , Tyler Derr , Ryan A. Rossi
papers.abstract: AI co-scientists that generate hypotheses, retrieve related work, design experiments, execute code, and draft full papers are beginning to change how research is carried out. Despite this rapid progress, state-of-the-art systems remain researcher-agnostic: given a research goal, they optimize novelty, validity, or reviewer score while ignoring the individual scientist who will use the output. This overlooks a fundamental fact about research, namely, that what counts as novel, valuable, or feasible depends on the researcher, including their prior work, methodological repertoire, and the collaborators and communities in which they are embedded. In this work, we introduce the problem of personalized auto-research, which conditions every stage of the research process on a representation of the individual researcher. We argue that personalization is not a convenience layer, but rather the fundamental property that allows an AI system to serve as a genuine co-scientist rather than a generic instrument. To address this problem, we propose a general and flexible framework that threads a graph-grounded researcher context through retrieval, hypothesis search, experimentation, writing, and review. The framework consists of three fundamental components: (i) graph-grounded researcher representations, (ii) personalization across the full research pipeline, and (iii) evaluation grounded in the individual. Notably, we highlight a one-size-fits-all failure mode where distinct researchers issuing the same goal receive essentially the same research, erasing the tacit knowledge through which novel ideas arise. Finally, we discuss fundamental open problems and challenges.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses personalized auto-research, which aligns with my interest in research agents for scientific discovery. The framework for conditioning research on researcher context could be applied to astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper introduces the problem of personalized auto-research, where AI co-scientists tailor every stage of research to an individual researcher. The main idea is a framework that uses graph-grounded researcher representations to personalize retrieval, hypothesis search, experimentation, writing, and review. For astronomy, this is highly relevant because it could create agents that understand an astronomer's prior work and methods, improving discovery. A concrete workflow could be a co-scientist that suggests new analyses for JWST data based on an astronomer's past papers. The main caveat is that the framework is conceptual, with no implementation or evaluation, so practical benefits are unproven.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the paper provides any concrete examples of personalization in a scientific domain
Look for a discussion of how to represent researcher context, such as publication graphs or code repositories

papers.title: Historical Backtesting for Scientific Question Discovery: A Protocol and Astronomy Pilot
papers.subjects: Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
papers.abstract: Systems that generate scientific research questions are evaluated today by expert scores, LLM-as-judge ratings, or curated case studies -- all subjective, none falsifiable. We formalize historical backtesting as an alternative: a system generates questions from a corpus frozen at a historical cutoff, the questions are frozen before any access to later literature, and a temporally isolated future corpus then determines whether each question was subsequently answered, partially addressed, independently posed, or ignored, and whether its underlying premise was supported or refuted. The protocol is model-agnostic: any system that emits frozen questions can be scored. We release reproducible astronomy instances with temporally isolated corpora, frozen questions, auditable labels, four reference baselines, and a submission interface. Two findings result. First, evidence-structure-first generation outperforms LLM-only prompting: across a generator decomposition crossed with a four-cutoff stress test (2010-2024, 798 judged questions) whose last window postdates model training, LLM-only generation shows memorized relevance without specific foresight, while a generator using no model weights at all finds questions whose premises the future refutes in every era. Second, a seven-rater agreement study (two blinded human annotators, five judge models, 90 items) indicts the outcome taxonomy rather than the judge: two careful humans agree at kappa = 0.17, every judge model agrees with the professional annotator as well or better (0.17-0.26), and frontier models agree with one another at 0.60 -- certifying an LLM judge by model-model agreement would have overstated its reliability threefold. A prospective instance -- 200 questions frozen 2026-08-17, scored 2027-2030 -- is released so the central claims become contamination-free tests that time itself will grade.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly targets automated scientific question discovery with a falsifiable evaluation protocol, highly relevant to research agents and scientific discovery in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the problem of evaluating AI systems that generate scientific research questions, proposing a historical backtesting protocol where questions are frozen before future literature is available and scored against that future. The main idea is to use temporally isolated corpora to objectively determine if generated questions were answered, refuted, or ignored, avoiding subjective expert scores. For astronomy, this could help build and validate AI-driven research agents that propose novel, testable questions for JWST or survey data. A concrete workflow would be to use this protocol to benchmark an LLM-based question generator on high-redshift galaxy or AGN topics. However, the low inter-rater agreement on the outcome taxonomy suggests that the evaluation labels themselves need careful design before trusting results.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the exact definition of the outcome taxonomy (answered, partially addressed, etc.) and how it handles ambiguous cases
Look for the released astronomy instances and whether they include JWST-era topics
Assess the generator decomposition (evidence-structure-first vs LLM-only) and whether it can be applied to my own question-generation pipelines

papers.title: HyMem: Hierarchical Context Management for Long-Horizon Agents via Information Isolation
papers.authors: XinQi Wang , Jinwei Xiao , Sijia Cui , Hongming Zhang , Yanna Wang , Qingyang Zhang , Bo Xu
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents often perform poorly on complex, long-horizon tasks because their context becomes increasingly cluttered over time. As interactions accumulate, detailed execution traces and intermediate outputs dominate the context, making it difficult for the model to retain and use high-level planning information. Most existing methods address this issue through compression or retrieval applied to a single, flat context, which does not clearly separate different types of context information and often leads to degraded reasoning. To address this challenge, we propose HyMem, a hierarchical framework that explicitly separates the agent's context into distinct functional layers. HyMem organizes context by function to separate high-level planning from execution and complex analysis. Its isolated reasoning module handles complex subtasks without adding intermediate reasoning traces to the persistent planning context, while its memory management module preserves task progress across context refreshes through structured summaries. These components reduce redundant context accumulation, retain task-critical information, and support coherent long-horizon reasoning within a limited context window. Experiments on GAIA and Browsecomp-plus show that, with DeepSeek-V4, HyMem achieves average Pass@1 scores of 66.7% and 61.3%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.1 and 4.7 percentage points, respectively. Further analysis indicates that HyMem effectively controls the growth of the reasoning context, allowing the model to maintain focus and accuracy across complex, long-horizon tasks.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses long-horizon agent context management, which is key for research agents in astronomy that must handle complex multi-step analyses and literature reviews. The hierarchical context separation could improve reliability of LLM-driven scientific workflows.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the problem of LLM agents losing track of high-level goals when their context fills with execution details over long tasks. It introduces HyMem, a framework that separates context into functional layers—planning, execution, and reasoning—so that intermediate steps don't clutter the persistent plan. For astronomy, this could help an agent maintain a clear research plan while running many data-analysis steps, e.g., fitting SEDs or querying catalogs. I could imagine using it to build a research agent that iteratively analyzes JWST spectra while keeping the original science question in focus. However, the method is tested on general benchmarks (GAIA, Browsecomp-plus), not scientific tasks, so I should check if the hierarchical design transfers to domain-specific workflows with long tool-use chains.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the hierarchical context design is model-agnostic and can be applied to open-source LLMs used in astronomy
Look for ablation studies showing which component (planning vs. reasoning isolation) contributes most to performance gains
See if the memory management module supports structured summaries of astronomical data products (e.g., spectra, images) or only text

papers.title: SEER: Long-Context Reasoning via Selective Visual-Text Compression
papers.authors: Jiawei Xu , Zhilin Zhai , Jinrui Fang , Ruohan Xu , Mingfei Lu , Yi Zhang , Guanchu Wang , Tianlong Chen , Ying Ding
papers.subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
papers.abstract: Long-context reasoning remains computationally expensive for large language models due to the quadratic complexity of attention over text tokens. Visual-text compression offers a promising alternative by rendering text into images and processing them with vision-language models, often reducing token usage. However, existing approaches apply uniform compression regardless of query relevance, potentially sacrificing precision where detailed extraction is required. We present SEER, a framework that learns to select query-relevant images through visual scanning and retrieve textual content only where needed, combining the efficiency of visual compression with the precision of text-based reasoning. Through supervised fine-tuning on tool-interaction trajectories, SEER learns adaptive tool invocation for selection and retrieval. Experiments on long-context benchmarks show that SEER improves extraction precision through selective text retrieval while retaining average prompt-token savings relative to full-text baselines. On LongBench, SEER achieves 51.11% average accuracy, outperforming the visual-text baseline Glyph-9B by 2.33 points and Qwen3-8B by 3.49 points. Code can be accessed at this https URL
papers.Reasons for match: The paper addresses long-context reasoning with selective visual-text compression, which could be relevant for processing large astronomical datasets or documents, but the application is generic and not astronomy-specific.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the computational cost of long-context reasoning in LLMs by selectively compressing text into images and retrieving text only where needed. The main idea is a framework that learns to choose query-relevant images through visual scanning, balancing efficiency and precision. This could matter for astronomy by enabling efficient processing of long multi-wavelength catalogs or literature, but the method is not validated on scientific data. A concrete workflow could be compressing long astronomical survey descriptions for question-answering agents. A caveat is that the compression may lose fine details needed for precise scientific analysis.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method can handle domain-specific text like astronomical papers or data descriptions.
Look for any evaluation on long documents with technical jargon or tables.
